Multidisciplinary treatment of non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) andprior trials of postoperative radiotherapy (PORT)
Surgical resection isamainstay of treatment for operable NSCLC. Patients with resected stage

I disease (per AJCC 9 ) are more often than not cured by local therapy alone. Those with resected stage II or higher disease benefit from the addition of adjuvant chemotherapy, and in biomarker- defined groups, the addition of additional therapies including immunotherapy or targ eted therapy.

Whether PORT can benefit patients with surgically resected NSCLC has been the topic of decades of clinical research. The PORT meta-analysis, published in 1998 and including trials published as early as 1980, showed an adverse effect of PORT on survival, except in N2 (ipsilateral mediastinal nodal) disease where there wasno clear evidence of an adverse effect.

Because the data in the case of N2 disease were equivocal and given ongoing technological improvements in the delivery of radiotherapy (RT), investig ators sought evidence that PORT is beneficial in the case of N2 disease. This included the Lung ART trial, which showed no significant improvement in disease-free survival with PORT (3-year DFS 47% with PORT vs. 44% without). Similarly, the
PORT-C trial showed no significant improvement in DFS (3-year DFS 40.5% with PORT vs.
% without, p=.20). Given the level 1 data, PORT for p N2 disease is no longer routinely recommended.
Benefits vs. risks of traditional PORT
In the Lung ART trial, those in the PORT group had substantially fewer mediastinal relapses (25%) compared to those in the control group (46%), and so one would anticipate a DFS benefit.

However, there was substantially higher late grade 3-4 cardiopulmonarytoxicity in the PORT group (11%) vs. control group (5%), and there were 16 deaths due to cardiopulmonary disease in the PORT group vs. 2 in the control group. Importantly to note, the volumes treated in the

Lung ART study included large portions of theheart and lungs; the clinical target volume (CTV) included all pathologically involved nodal stations, any intervening stations, plus ipsilateral paratracheal (level 4), subcarinal (level 7), and ipsilateral hilar (level 10) stations regardless of involveme nt, plus bronchial stump. On top of this, there wasaplanning target volume (PTV) expansion of CTV + 0.5 -1 cm. 3D

In PORT-C, there wasapoor rate of treatment compliance, however there wasasubstantially lower rate of cardiopulmonary toxicity in this study in which most patients were treated with intensity modulated RT (IMRT). While the primary intention-to-treat DFS endpoint was negative, secondary analyses on the per-protocol and as-treated populations did demonstrate significantly improved DFS with PORT.

Oligoprogression on first -line ICI +/ - chemotherapy systemic therapy after at least 3 cycles.
Oligoprogression is evaluated independently for each lesion, and will be defined as follows
Modified Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumours (RECIST 1.1 [Eisenhauer 2009] )

1) At least a 20% increase in the longest diameter (LD) ofalesion except for lymph nodes where only the short axis is measured, taking as reference the smallest LD/short axis recorded since nadir, and ≥ 5 mm increase in the LD/short axis, OR;
2) The appearance of one or more new lesions, each ≥ 5 mm in size. OR
Modified Positron Emission Tomography Response Criteria in Solid Tumours (PERCIST [Wahl 2009] )
1) >30% increase in 18F FDG SUV max, with >0.8 SUV units increase in tumour SUV from previous baseline scan in pattern typical of tumour and not of infection/treatment effect, OR;
2) Visible increase in the extent of 18F-FDG tumour uptake, OR;
3) New 18F-FDG avid lesions typical of cancer (including new bone lesion) and not related to treatment effect and/or infection.

There is no upper limit to the number of total metastatic sites, butamaximum of 5 progressive metastatic sites, inclusive of primary disease and metastatic lesions, all of which must be extracranial. CONFIDENTIAL 14 CONFIDENTIAL PROTOCOL - UPDATE #7: 2026-JAN-07

All sites of oligoprogression can be safely treated with SBRT or ablative radiotherapy as determined by the treating radiation oncologist, including availability and tolerability of necessary technologies (e.g. active breathing control, MRLinac, fiducial insertion, etc.) and accounting for previous radiotherapy overlap. Safety must be assessed and determined byaradiation oncologist prior to enrollment.

Participants with treated CNS disease who have radiologic and clinical evidence of stable brain metastases, with no evidence of cavitation or hemorrhage in the brain lesion, are eligible providing that they are asymptomatic and do not require corticostero ids (must have discontinued steroids at least 1 week prior to randomization). Candidate for regulatory approved SOC first-line or second-line systemic therapy options.
Participants must have adequate organ and marrow function according to the relevant systemic therapies’ current Product Monographs and local / provincial / institutional formulary guidelines.
Participants must be ≥ 18 years of age.
ECOG performance status of 0, 1 or 2.

eligibility: Pleasesee Section 4 of the Master EN.10 Protocol, as well as additional sub-study specific criteria described in the EN.10 sub-study sections of the master protocol. Additional information is also available in the EN.10 Pathology Instructions document provided on the CCTG trial specific website and the CTSU website.
Prior to inclusion in this trial, complete molecular classification must be performed on an

EC specimen. This can be either the tumor-containing hysterectomy specimen or the preoperative specimen. Molecular classification includes mutational status assessment of the exonuclease domain of DNA polym erase epsilon ( POLE ), MMR-IHC, estrogen receptor (ER)-IHC, and p53-IHC or TP53 sequencing. The test should be performed in a (pathology) laboratory with accreditation to report clinically validated results by
International Accreditation New Zealand or equivalent. MMR, ER, and p53 IHC testing, and interpretation will be performed locally at each participating center. Centers requiring

POLE sequencing to be performed at another approved site should ship FFPE block, at ambient temperature to that site. Samples sent for testing should consist of the highest viable tumor cells for optimal assay performance. All molecular tests should be completed promptly to ensure patients can be treated or offered active surveillance wit hin 10 weeks of hysterectomy and staging.

Alternatively, the protocol allows flexibility in utilizing different commercial next generation sequencing (NGS) companies to provide services in order to increase the availability of participation in this trial. These companies provide services throughout the country and are not confined to regional or institution type (i.e. academic vs community practice). Molecular classification by NGS is acceptable so long as
HIV-infected patients on effective anti-retroviral therapy with undetectable viral load within 6 months are eligible for this trial.

The starting dose/schedule (level 3) included full dose pembrolizumab (200 mg IV), first administered the week prior to the start of CRT and then every 3 weeks foratotal of 8 doses, cisplatin 40 mg/m 2 /week during IMRT, and 6 weeks of conventionally fractionated IMRT to 60 Gy.
This schedule included full overlap of pembrolizumab with cisplatin and IMRT.

For the duration of the studyfrom Nov ember 2016 to Oct ober 2018, 34 eligible patients were enrolled at 22 NRG Oncology institutions. During the first cohort, 1 DLT was observed (Grade 3 fever). RP2S was declared as Schedule 3 and the expansion cohort was triggered. Among all 34 enrolled patients, median age was 60 y ea rs ( range 26-83); 68% were male; 74% had a Zubrod performance status of 1; 85% had an oral

The starting dose and schedule (level 3), as depicted in Figure 2, is the recommended phase II dose and schedule for the combination of adjuvant pembrolizumab, cisplatin, and IMRT for the adjuvant management of pathologic high risk, HPV-negative HNSCC.
Atezolizumab (MPDL3280A, NSC# 783608, IND# 138328)

Atezolizumab isaphage-derived human Ig G1 m Ab against PD-L1. The Fc domain of atezolizumab was engineered to eliminate antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity (ADCC) or complement-dependent cytotoxicity (CDC) thereby preventing the depletion of T cells expressing
PD-L1 (Lee 2017). Atezolizumab is FDA approved in locally advanced or metastatic urothelial carcinoma. Atezolizumab has been evaluated as monotherapy in refractory, recurrent/metastatic

HNSCC and demonstrated an overall response rate of 22%, PFS of 2.6 months, and median OS of 6.0 months, in line with phase I res ults from anti-PD1 m Ab (Colevas 2018). Maintenance atezolizumab after completion of definitive RT for locally advanced HNSCC is now under study inaphase III randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT03452137).
Cumulative data from phase I, II, and III studies across multiple solid tumor types indicate that

PD-1 and PD-L1 m Ab are similar in both toxicity profile and clinical activity. The interest of NRG is in adding a PD-1 or PD-L1 m Ab to adjuvant cisplatin-IMRT in high risk, HPV-negative HNSCC; however, we are agnostic as to the specific m Ab.

Given the class toxicity profile of anti-PD1/L1 m Ab, the safety of the combination of atezolizumab, cisplatin, and IMRT in the high-risk adjuvant setting is inferred from NRG HN003. This inference is further supported by phase I data in the definitive setting now available in the public domain, including

Gillison and colleagues reported the results of RTOG Foundation 3504, a multi-arm phase I trial adding nivolumab to definitive RT backbones (Gillison 2018). Nivolumab was safe and feasible to administer concurrently with cisplatin-IMRT, where cisplatin was dosed at 40 mg/m 2 /week or at 100 mg/m 2 every 3 weeks.

Powell and colleagues reported an interim safety analysis including 27 patients onaphase Ib trial of the combination of pembrolizumab 200 mg every 3 weeks, cisplatin 40 mg/m 2/week, and IMRT in the definitive setting for locally advanced HNSCC (Powell 2016). The immune- related toxicity rate in these 27 patients was no different from pembrolizumab monotherapy, and the regimen was both tolerable and feasible.
1. 5 Importance of This Trial ( 20-MAR-2020 )

Initial Design: The proposed randomized phase II-III trial will address several important issues in head and neck cancer. Approximately 50% of head and neck cancer patients undergo primary surgery for their malignancy. For those with high-risk clinical and pathologic features ( eg bone destruction, extracapsular nodal extension, tumor involving resection margins) [Peters 1993; Ang

2001; Bernier 2005), the local-regional failure rates remain high and efforts to reduce recurrence include the use of postoperati ve radiation, and more recently, postoperative chemoradiation. The beneficial impact of adding cisplatin chemotherapy to radiation in the high-risk setting is modest and is accompanied by significant incremental toxicity (including ototoxicity, nephrotoxicity, neutropenia, nausea, and

This study will therefore address the question whether docetaxel alone is as active as docetaxel and cetuximab combination and whether either taxane-based regimen is better than cisplatin monotherapy given to this high-risk group of patients with concurrent radiation. The less toxic weekly cisplatin regimen is selected to enhance compliance in the control arm and to parallel to weekly regimen proposed for the 2

Merged Design: The amended phase III design addsthe NRG-HN003 regimen (cisplatin-IM RT + anti-PD1 or PDL1 m Ab) asathird arm to RTOG 1216 when it re-opens to Phase III. Fromadrug development standpoint, the major goal is to telescope the development of an anti-PD1/PDL1 m Ab in the high-risk adjuvant space. This recommendation stems from the 2014 NCI/CTEP and
HN Steering Committee’s Clinical Trials Planning Meeting, entitled Immunotherapy of Head and

Neck Cancer (Bauman 2017). Given the poor overall outcomes for this curative-intent patient population, and the groundbreaking outcomes for anti-PD1 immunotherapy in the recurrent/ metastatic setting, this was recommended asahigh priority.
In order to efficiently address the immunotherapy question in this patient population, a new phase
III comparison of adjuvant CRT +/-atezo lizumab is being added to the phase III component of
RTOG 1216 asamajor amendment. The merged phase III design has the following advantages

1) Significant head start. Allowsaphase III trial evaluating theaddition of a PD1 or PDL1 m Ab to cisplatin-IMRT in the high-risk adjuvant space to start in 2019. Whereas, serial phase III designs would require deferring trial start until at least 2023.
2) Design efficiency. Leverages the use ofacommon control arm (cisplatin-IMRT) dur ing the period of joint accrual.

3) Two independent phase III comparisons. Two primary phase III comparisons of OS will be conducted: a) cisplatin-IMRT vs. docetaxel-cetuximab-IMRT; b) cisplatin-IMRT vs. atezolizumab plus cisplatin-IMRT.

By the use of this efficient merged design, both human and fiscal resources are appropriately governed within the NCTN portfolio. There is no competing trial in the adjuvant, high risk space within the NCTN or industry.

eligibility: Histologic cT2-T4aN0M0 muscle-invasive urothelial carcinoma of the bladder within 180 days before neoadjuvant therapy starts. Staging CT, MRI, or PET of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis within 60 days before neoadjuvant therapy.

After neoadjuvant therapy, a repeat TURBT must show cT0 or cT1. It biopsies the prior disease and systematic sites (left and right lateral walls, dome, posterior wall, and trigone), with at least 4 of 5 systematic biopsies. At least 3 and no more than 6 cycles of FDA-approved neoadjuvant therapy: cisplatin-based combination chemotherapy, with or without a PD-1/L1 inhibitor; dose-dense or accelerated MVAC; or enfortumab vedotin with a PD-1/L1 inhibitor.
No small cell, neuroendocrine, or plasmacytoid histology. Mixed histology is allowed when more than half of the tumor is urothelial carcinoma. No prior pelvic radiotherapy.

For patients with metastatic HER2 negative gastroesophageal adenocarcinoma, a current NCCN preferred standard first line therapy is doublet chemotherapy with FOLFOX. FOLFOX. First-line FOLFOX achievesamedian progression-free survival (m PFS) time of about 6 months andamedian overall survival (OS) of about 11 months. Given this modest benefit, multiple trials have evaluated FOLFIRINOX regimen in this setting.

Evolution in thestandard of care

Prostate cancer (PC) is the second most common cancer and fifth leading cause of cancer death in men worldwide 1. Androgen deprivation therapy (ADT) has been the backbone of therapy for systemic castrate-sensitive prostate cancer (C SPC ) since its discovery in 19412. Docetaxel became the only cytotoxic agent with proven survival benefit in prostate cancer when its efficacy in castration-resistant disease was

The PEACE-1 and ARASENS trials explored the role of ADT plus docetaxel +/-ARSI and noted an improvement in overall survival ( OS ) with the addition of either abiraterone acetate or darolutamide, respectively 8,9. However, neither study showed that docetaxel itself impacted survival or identifiedasubgroup of patients who benefited from treatment with docetaxel. The

PEACE-1 trial included only men with de novo metastatic disease and it was observed that the addition of abiraterone acetate to ADT and docetaxel backbone improved radiographic progression free survival (r PFS) and OS in the entire population. Subgroup analysis demonstrated the benefit of abiraterone acetate in terms of r PFS in both low-and high-volume patients and OS benefit only in high-volume patients only.

In the ARASENS trial, ofthe 1,305 patients, 1,005 (77%) had high-volume disease and 912 (70%) had high-risk disease. In contrast to the PEACE-1 trial, this study allowed men with recurrent PC to be enrolled and this group constituted close to 15% of the entire study population. Primary plasma cell leukemia (PCL) is an aggressive variant of multiple myeloma associated with dismal prognosis and lack ofastandard of care therapeutic approach. As such, it is generally considered the most difficult plasma cell neoplasm to treat and control. The annual incidence of PCL is 0.04 cases per

100,000 [1] and occurs in 2-4% of all multiple myeloma (MM) cases based on historical PCL diagnostic criteria (> 20% circulating PCs). Given that survival outcomes are similar between those defined as PCL with > 20% and > 5% circulating plasma cells, the diagnostic criteria have now been updated [2, 3] to define primary plasma cell leukemia ( p PCL ) as those patients having ≥ 5% circulating plasma cells.

Therefore, the incidence of PCL is likely higher than previously accepted [4]. PCL is characterized by high-risk disease features including extramedullary disease, hypercalcemia, cytopenias, and renal failur e

[4]. Though poorly understood on the molecular level, up to 50% of patients with p PCL harbor the (11;14) translocation with or without high-risk genomic features including del (17p), increased copies of

1q21, and deletion of 1p32 [5-7]. Those patients that harbor t (11;14) generally live twice as long as those without (39.2 vs 17.9 months) and this is associated withacorresponding 3-year overall survival of 60% and 25% for t (11;14) and non-t (11;14) patients [6], respectively ( Figure 1 ); p PCL with t (11;14) is thought to represent different underlying disease biology than that seen in patients who do not have t

The therapeutic options available for patients with MM have greatly expanded over the past decade and incorporating these novel agents into routine clinical practice has significantly improved outcomes. The next generation of therapeutics are available for relapsed and refractory patients either as standard of care or in clinical trials, and these drugs representagenerational paradigm shift. Rationale for selected approach and trial design
Metastatic non-small cell lung cancer claims far more lives than any other cancer diagnosis.

Although surgically resectable non-small cell lung cancer is considered curable, many th experience recurrence of disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy post resection of stage IB-IIIA (7 edition) NSCLC is an established standard of care that improves DFS and OS, but unfortunately many patients experience relapse that impacts survival. A regimen that reduces recurrence rates after surgical resection of early stage NSCLC

There have been significant advances in the treatment of non-small cell lung cancer, particularly the addition of checkpoint inhibitors to the armamentarium of treatment options. Checkpoint inhibitors are established in the treatment of stage IV disease andapprov ed in stage III post 3-5 treatment with concurrent chemotherapy and radiation for surgically unresectable disease.
The addition of pembrolizumab to chemotherapy in the front-line setting of non-squamous

NSCLC significantly improves PFS and OS. A phase 3 trial of chemotherapy alone vs combination pembrol izumab revealed an improvement in PFS and OS with the combination in patients with squamous NSCLC. This new intensified standard of care may have particular benefit in the adjuvant setting whereagreater impact on cancer has the potential to eliminate all remaining cancer cells. Although an intensified regimen would

Due to the value that has been demonstrated in the metastatic setting, there are trials underway investigating the addition ofacheckpoint inhibitor sequentially following standard of care chemotherapy. These trials include eligible patients after complet ion of any planned chemotherapy. Due to the timing of enrollment, these protocols select out those with poor performance status, complications related to adjuvant
IMpower-010 demonstrated improvement in DFS with atezolizumab after adj uvant chemotherapy compared to adjuvant chemotherapy alone in those with stage II-IIIA and PD-L1
>1% leading to FDA approval in that population. Further analysis including those with <1%
PD-L1 expression and earlier stage are pending maturation of the study.

We plan treatment of stage I IA-III B (T3-4N2) non-small cell lung cancer post-resection to evaluate the impact of pembrolizumab, a PD-1 inhibitor, when added to standard of care adjuvant therapy, evaluating 2 different strategies. We started the study with randomiz ation to one of three arms: 1) chemotherapy alone followed by observation (control) 2) chemotherapy alone for 4 cycles followed by pembrolizumab for 17

Protocol Update #7, after FDA approval of sequential atezolizumab, includes randomization to the 2 experimental arms (B and C). In 2025, an estimated 226, 650 adults in the United States will be diagnosed with lung 12,3 cancer. At least 31.8% of these new cases (≈ 72,000) will have stage I NSCLC. The actual incidence is likely to be higher as the stage at diagnosis continues to shift towards an early- stage lung cancer, with the increased adoption of lung cancer screening guidelines. From
2010 to 2017, there is an increase in stage I NSCLC at diagn osis from 25.9% to 31.8%.
Standard of care for patients with stage I NSCLC is complete surgical resection. Patients who cannot undergo surgery, usually receive stereotactic ablative radiotherapy (SABR).

Previous studies have shown that relapse rates for st age I non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) can range from 16-38% following the surgical resection, and the 5-year overall survival for clinical stage IA and IB NSCLC is 68-92%. While adjuvant chemotherapy has proven toimprove disease-free and overall survival for patients with completely resected stage II and IIIA NSCLC, there is no evidence that adjuvant chemotherapy improves outcomes for patients with resected stage I NSCLC (tumors < 4 cm). Therefore, the standard of care for stage I NSCLC (tumors < 4 cm), after complete resection is active surveillance if there is no actionable gene

Recently, IMpower010 and KN091 trials have shown an improvement in disease-free survival (DFS) of patients with stage II-IIIA resected NSCLC. Treatment Challenges in Platinum Refractory Disease

Patients with platinum refractory disease have limited treatment options and are excluded from most clinical trials: In locally advanced HNSCC, cisplatin is used asastandard of care concurrently with radiation therapy (CRT) in the definitive, non-operative setting or in the adjuvant setting following surgery. Platinum refractory disease is defined as the developmentof disease progression within 6 months on or

Historically, platinum refractory HNSCC disease is observed in ~10-20% of patients treated in the curative setting and haveamedian overall survival of <6 months. A Japanese study showed that 38% HNSCC patients had platinum refractory disease following CRT with cisplatin (842/2212 patients). The same study showed that platinum rechallenge in 300/842 (36%) patients resulted in poor clinical activity and tolerability

This data highlights two critical problems: a) A larger percentage of platinum refractory HNSCC may exist than previously reported. b) Despite poor response to platinum re-challenge, clinical practice is heterogenous with providers continuing to use platinum-based regimens despite poor tolerability and efficacy.
Furthermore, p atients with platinum refractory disease have been excluded from on-going clinical trials evaluating novel therapeutic combinations in R/M HNSCC.

Rural cancer survivors are atahigh risk of tobacco-related morbidity and mortality and decreased quality of life compared to their non-rural counterparts. [1, 2] Cancer survivors who quit smoking reduce their risk of subsequent primary cancer [3] and increase their treatment efficacy, [4] survival, [5,

6] and quality of life (QOL). [7, 8] Yet, rural cancer survivors who want to quit have relatively poor access to cessation interventions. [1] Available interventions for cancer survivors have not been very effective, and most require multiple face-to-face appointments, which isahardship for many rural survivors. New approaches to reach rural cancer survivors are needed. One such approach isatext- based Scheduled

Delivering the intervention via text-messaging eliminates the need for mu ltiple burdensome clinic visits and increases reach and access. Text messaging isamethod that has strong potential to deliver tobacco cessation interventions given its availability, low cost, and widespread use even in rural areas.
Yet to date no studies have examinedatext-based SGR ces sation approach with rural cancer survivors.
A text-based SGR approach has the potential to be superior to current cessation interventions for cancer survivors for the following reasons

1) SGR helps smokers learn to refrain from smoking in response to environmental cues by giving individualsasmoking schedule that gradually reduces their use to zero. Learning to self-regulate smoking in response to behavioral cues helps smokers develop copi ng skills to deal with cravings and urges. These coping skills are imperative for cessation success among cancer survivors as cravings are cited asaprimary
2) SGR helps mitigate withdrawal symptoms common in highly dependent smokers such as tension, fatigue, and urges to smoke by gradual ly weaning nicotine, usingasmoking reduction schedule. [13, 14]

3) SGR helps build self-efficacy. As smokers meet reduction goals, they become more confident in their ability to quit. This is important as cancer survivors’ low self-efficacy decreases their odds of quitting. [7, 8, 13, 14] Further, through this increased self-efficacy for behavior change positive, “spillover effects” may be obse rved for other health behaviors. [15]

4) Only about one-third of cancer survivors who smoke want to quit smoking immediately, yet all interventions focus on abrupt quitting by asking patients to set quit dates within 2 weeks to 30 days. Given that two-thirds of cancer patients who smoke are notready to quit immediatelyareduction approach may beamore efficacious and acceptable approach. [16]

A paradigm shift is underway from early detection of individual cancers to simultaneous early detection of multiple cancers withasingle blood draw. This is possible through analysis of circulating tumor cell-free DNA (cf DNA) and leveraging genomic techno logies, machine learning, and/or logistic regression algorithms to simultaneously detect multiple cancers and accurately predict the tissue of origin. Such an
Evolving methods to analyze cell free nucleic acids in the peripheral blood have achieved the level of sensitivity needed to realize the possibility of multicancer early detection through blood.

THRIVE’s Cancer SEEK assay usesalogistic regression algorithmthat accounts for multiplexed PCR detection of 16 selected mutations and measurements of validated protein biomarkers that relies on cross-sectional whole body imaging to identify the anatomic primary site [1, 2]. GRAIL’s Galleri test isatargeted methylation bisulfite sequencing assay coupled with machine learning to reportageneral cancer signal as well

Collectively, there is an opportunity for MCED testing to reduce cancer mortality and treatment costs, improve the effectiveness of cancer screening, and complement single-cancer screening approaches.

We are optimistic that findings from future population-based trials in intended-use populations will identify proper workflows for test implementation and facilitate the adoption of MCED tests in clinical practice. However, blinded validation of reported sensitivity and specificity should be pursued before ind ividual assays are considered for incorporation into clinical utility studies.

There are >140,000 new cases of colorectal cancer (CRC) each year in the
United States, of which 25% present with isolated metastases to the liver and 50- 1-4

Surgical resection has the greatest impact on patient survival for metastases limited to the liver, which yields a 5-year survival rate up to 60% and is curative in 5,67
~20 %. However, less than 25% of patients are candidates for surgery.

Patients with unresectable colorectal liver metastases (CRLM) are generally treated with systemic chemotherapy, often in combination with other liver- directed therapies (e.g., trans-arterial embolotherapy, ablation, or radiation).

First-line chemotherapy, most commonly FOLFOX or FOLFIRI which are considered to be similarly effective, may facilitate resection of initially inoperable 8-17 disease, however, survival for all patients is only 15-31 months. General Background and Rationale

Aggressive B-cell lymphomas, most commonly diffuse large B-cell lymphoma 1-3 (DLBCL), can be cured with initial combination chemoimmunotherapy; however, those with refractory disease and those with early relapse following high-dose chemotherapy and autologous stem cell transplantation (HDT/ASCT) have particularly dismal outcomes with standard therapies, withamedian survival of approximately 6 m onths.

Identification of key survival pathways in lymphoid malignancies and development of drugs that target those pathways has resulted in recent therapeutic advances. Novel targeted therapies have emerged that can disrupt key survival pathways in lymphoma such as regulation of apoptosis ( BCL2: venetoclax), B-cell receptor signaling (BTK: ibrutinib), and NF-κB survival pathways (IRF4/SPIB: lenalidomide; NF-κB:

A major limitation of targeted therapy is the current use of long-term continuous dosing schedules, which precludes combining multiple agents due to cumulative toxicity. In contrast, intermittent dosing limits toxicities and potentially allows combination targeted regimens, akin to combination cytotoxic regimens. Indeed, if these targeted agents undermine multiple essential survival mechanisms in the tumor cells and
Usingahigh-throughput screening platform, the Bruton’s tyrosine kinase (BTK) inhibitor, ibrutinib, has been shown to synergistically inhibit the growth of ABC

DLBCL cell lines when combined with multiple targeted agents as well as standard chemotherapy. Specifically, within the BCL2 family inhibitors, greater synergy has been observed with ibrutinib in combination with venetoclax (ABT
199) than was seen with navitoclax in all ABC DLBCL cell lines tested.

Furthermore, the immunomodulatory agent (i MID) len alidomide has also shown significant synergy with ibrutinib in killing ABC DLBCL cell lines through downregulation of IRF4 and SPIB transcription factors, leading to decreased NF- κB signaling and promotion of IFN  production. Based on the above synergy observed in pre-clinical testing, the National Cancer

Institute (NCI) conductedasingle-center, phase 1b/2 study of venetoclax, ibrutinib, prednisone, obinutuzumab, and lenalidomide (Revlimid®) (i.e., Vi POR) in relapsed/refracto ry B-cell lymphomas (Clinical Trials.gov Identifier

NCT03223610), and demonstrated that the combination of Vi POR was safe and 13,14 tolerated by patients of all ages. Hematologic adverse events (AEs), mainly neutropenia, were most common and manageable with G-CSF support, with G3

Non-hematologic AEs were less common and mainly G1-2 in severity with the only G3-4 non-hematologic AEs observed in

>5% of patients being hypokalemia, diarrhea, and atrial fibrillation in 28%, 8%, and 5% of patients, respectively. G3-4 rash occurred likely secondary to the intermittent, cyclicdosing schedule and concomitant use of corticosteroids. Only

Myelodysplastic syndromes (MDS) areaheterogenous group of clonal myeloid disorders characterized by clonal expansion of hematopoietic stem cells, ineffective hematopoiesis, andavariable risk of progression to acute myeloid leukemia (AML) [1]. The Revised International

Prognostic Scoring System (IPSS-R) serves asarisk stratification tool to identify lower-risk disease versus higher-risk disease while providing overall survival (OS) estimates along with risk of progression to AML [2]. An IPSS-R score of ≥ 4 is considered to be higher-risk MDS due to increased mortality and risk of progression to AML [3].
DNA-methyltransferase inhibitor (DNMTi) monotherapy currently represents the standard of care in higher-risk MDS. This standard was established byanumber of randomized controlled trials.

AML with rearrangements involving genes encoding subunits of core-binding factor (CBF), a group of DNA-binding transcription factor complexes, share similar pathogenesis and clinical features and are consideredadistinct subset of AML (1, 2). Translocatio n (8;21)(q22;q22) and inv (16)(p13q22) lead to the creation of the dominant negative fusion genes RUNX1::RUNXT1 and CBFB::MYH11 contributing to leukemogenesis.

The proposed study will determine if venetoclax can replace gemtuzumab ozogamicin (GO) as part of curative therapy for CBF-AML with standard 7+3 induction chemotherapy. While the addition of GO has increased the rate of CR MRD-in CBF-AML, GO is associated with significant toxicities including persistent thrombocytopenia and veno-occlusive disease/sinusoidal obstruction syndrome of the liver. Therefore, we seek to
AML may have differential sensitivity to venetoclax and GO, patients with RAS and/or KIT mutations will be evaluated separately.

Current standard management of CBF-AML consists of cytarabine and an anthracycline with many centers adding GO. The data supporting the use of GO does not allow discernment of whether this agent provides benefit in all molecular subsets. V enetoclax has been safely added to induction regimens in AML in phase II studies and results in very high rates of CR MRD-[6-8].
Therefore, a prospective examination of whether alternative regimens may be superior to GO in patients with CBF-AML is warranted.
CBF-AML blasts frequently harbor additional mutations; the most prevalent include KIT and
RAS. KIT mutations in exons 8 or 17 are found in both inv (16) and t (8;21) [1-6] ( Figure 1 ) and are associated with poor outcomes [5-8]. RAS mutations are very common (30-40%) in CBF
AML [1, 6, 9] ( Figure 1 ). Although shown not consistently by all studies [6], several studies suggest that mutant RAS is associated with poor prognosis in this group of AML patients [9

11]. Moreover, about 15% of patients have both KIT and RAS mutations [5]. Molecular analysis of the ALFA0701 study, which prospectively demonstrated the benefit of GO in induction therapy for better-risk AML patients (see below), suggests that the benefit of GO was largely restricted toagroup that had mutations in FLT3 or RAS. Inclusion of Understudied Populations
The incidence of new endometrial cancer diagnoses are relatively equal among non
Hispanic Black and White women at roughly 28 cases per 100,000. For Hispanic women, this rate is modestly lower at 25 cases/100,000. According to 2020 US census data, the non
Hispanic Black population in the age mostly likely affected by endometrial cancer is 12
15%, whereas the Hispanic population is 15-20%. As such, to overcome barriers for participation, we aim to enhance participation of in this trial by incorporating the following strategies

Strategy 1: We have deliberately designed liberal inclusion criteria which include all endometrial histologies, including high-risk histologies which disproportionatelyaffect Black and African American patients.

Strategy 2: We have extended inclusion to those with ECOG 0-2 performance status, such that participation of Black and Hispanic populations already disproportionately affected by access to care, systemic inequities and thus at higher risk for exclusionary comorbid conditions will not be dispropor tionately excluded from participation.
Strategy 3: We will provide both English and Spanish consentswhich will prevent the exclusion of non-English speaking Hispanic participants.
Strategy 4: We will target and actively promote opening this trial at NCORP sites located in regions in which Black and Hispanic populations are overrepresented compared to the general US population.

Strategy 5: The investigators will develop evidential content about endometrial cancer, specifically among racial/ethnic groups, for inclusion in recruitment materials and operational procedures for study enrollment. An evidential communication approach provides data that are specific to racial/et hnic groups; in this case, the evidential content will focus on racial gaps in endometrial cancer risk and survival. eligibility: Significance for Future Clinical Trials. Patients with cancer are increasingly using cannabis products, despite limited evidence for beneficial effects and largely unknown harms. This study will collaborate with the NCI Community Oncology Research Program (NCORP) and Alliance for Clinical Trials in

Oncology (ALLIANCE) to longitudinally assess the benefits and harms of cannabis and cannabinoid use among cancer patients in active treatment. These data will provideabetter understanding of the temporal relationship between heterogeneous patterns of cannabis and cannabino id use and cancer symptom management; information that will contribute significantly to the design of future clinical trials in cancer care.
